mbira 等舌簧琴（撥奏體鳴樂器）在非洲存在數千年，木或竹舌片約三千年前見於西: Lamellophones such as the mbira (plucked idiophones) have existed in Africa for millennia: wooden or bamboo tongues appear on the West African coast about three thousand years ago, and metal tongues appeared in the Zambezi valley about thirteen hundred years ago. The latter spread across the continent and developed different forms and social uses among the Shona of Zimbabwe and the peoples of Mozambique. In the mid-twentieth century the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey designed the kalimba on the model of the mbira nyunga nyunga and exported it, which took the instrument out of Africa; in the 1960s and early 1970s it became popular through Maurice White, Thomas Mapfumo and others playing it alongside modern rock instruments.

Its range usually spans two to three octaves: the top is clear and sweet, the low warm and full, and the middle most prominent and rounded. When the player plucks a metal tongue the sound begins in the tongue itself and is then reinforced and projected by the wooden resonator, producing a distinctive resonance, and each note has a clear decay curve. Beside the mechanical quality of the piano and the metallic sheen of the guitar, the thumb piano has a machine-like regularity and the warmth of a folk instrument. Its sound is softly penetrating, never harsh yet clearly carried, and often gives a meditative, relaxed listening experience, full of a raw and refined African musical aesthetic.

The thumb piano, also called mbira, kalimba or zanza, is a lamellophone originating with the Shona of Zimbabwe; it is a plucked idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs classification 122.1. It is built from a wooden board (often with a resonator) on which staggered metal tongues are fixed, and the player holds the instrument and plucks the tongues with the thumb or fingers. In eastern and southern Africa it is common in religious ritual, weddings and social gatherings, and it often plays with percussion such as the hosho.
拇指鋼琴（mbira、kalimba）屬撥奏體鳴／簧片體鳴樂器，Hornbost: The thumb piano (mbira, kalimba) is a plucked idiophone / lamellophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 122.1, traditional among the Shona and other peoples of Africa. Its body is a wooden board, often fitted with a resonator; the sounding bodies are staggered metal tongues, plucked with the thumb or fingers. The tongues were originally bamboo and later developed into metal keys. The source does not record the wood species, the resonator or the materials of the other parts.

On the modern stage it has also been set beside rock line-ups with electric guitar, bass, drum kit and brass, playing material drawn from the traditional repertory. In the United States there is also teaching and recording of the Shona mbira.

演奏時以雙手托住樂器，用拇指或手指撥動金屬舌片發聲。初學可先熟悉常見音位：最低音: Hold the instrument in both hands and pluck the metal tongues with the thumbs or fingers. Beginners can first learn the common layout: the lowest note is usually in the centre, with the higher notes to left and right, so that the thumbs can reach every tongue. In sound, the overtones of a plucked tongue are rather inharmonic, the attack is clear and the decay short, and neighbouring tongues also vibrate a little. When practising rhythm, start from the division of labour between the hands: the left hand keeps a fixed bass pattern and the right plays the melody above, together making a three-against-two cross rhythm. Tuning varies with the family or the instrument, so a beginner should learn the intervals as relative ones and not simply apply Western equal temperament.
